utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, may we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Alex Demirdjian, Stavroula Papadopoulous, Case Manager Thomas Laugel, legal intern Milomir Matovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. There's a short oral ruling. On the 25th of June, 2013, the Trial Chamber determined that the Defence had laid sufficient foundation for the admission of Exhibit D74 into evidence. However, the exhibit was MFI'd pending provision of a corrected English translation. On 9 October 2013, the Defence provided a corrected translation of the exhibit. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the current English translation of D74 with the version uploaded as document ID 1D05-1703, after which time the MFI status shall be lifted and D74 shall be deemed admitted into evidence. The Registry shall take any other necessary action to implement this decision. Could the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. First of all, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Demirdjian, I suppose we have a pseudonym sheet? Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: There are no protective measures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, sorry, there are no protective measures. Sorry, sir. Could you please tell us your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jovan Susic. Born on the 13th of April, 1957, in the village of Bukovica, municipality of Savnik, Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to make the solemn declaration, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out to you that by doing, so you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury, should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Could I now ask you to make the solemn declaration. The court usher will give you the text of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Susic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, it is correct to say that are you a retired colonel of the Yugoslavia People's Army which later became the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And is it right to say that testified here at the Tribunal in November of 2006 in the case of Mrksic, Radic, and Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in that case, you were called to testify during the Defence case of Veselin Sljivancanin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you testified for the better part of two days, that is, on the 17th and 20th of November, 2006?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now when you arrived here in The Hague a few days ago, were you given an opportunity to listen to the audio recording of your testimony in the Mrksic case?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I was, and I listened to the entire recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You actually pre-empted my next question which was to ask you if you listened it. You confirmed that now. Would you say that it is an accurate recording of the testimony you gave in the Mrksic case?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Fully. Fully accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you the same questions today would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I would give entirely the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage I would seek to tender 65 ter numbers 6481 and 6482. These are the two days of testimony of Mr. Susic in the Mrksic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3025, the under seal version, and public redacted version will be P3025.1. And 65 ter 6482 will be Exhibit P3026 under seal and the public redacted version will be P3026.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I had failed to mention that we had also a redacted version due to portions of the private session. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, your testimony in -- from the Mrksic case has now been admitted on the record. This means that we do not need to revisit all the details of your prior testimony. However, I do have a number of items I wish to get some clarifications from you. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony - and, for the record, that's at page 14887 - you mention Branislav Lukic as a commander of the 2nd Assault Detachment, and you also mention that he is the commander of the JNA barracks. Could you tell the Court when he -- when did he become the commander of the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: He became the commander of the barracks on the 2nd of November, 1991 -- sorry, the 2nd of October, yes, the 2nd of October, 1991. The 2nd of October, 1991, when I came to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when -- when he became commander of the JNA barracks, which units were stationed there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: The units of the 2nd Assault Detachment were stationed there. As well as an anti-terrorist company of the 1st Battalion of the military police. As of the 4th of October, the 2nd Company of the MP battalion was stationed there as well, which was also to provide security for the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just so that the Trial Chamber understand, when you say -- when we talk about the 2nd Assault Detachment, what are we talking about here? What kind of a unit is this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: It's the 2nd Battalion of the Guards Brigade which was also called the 2nd Assault Detachment. But it's one and the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now, you also mentioned in your testimony in the Mrksic case that your command post was in Negoslavci but that your forward command post was at the JNA barracks. Could you also tell us, for the record, as of when was your forward command post at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: As of the 1st of November, 1991. That was when the forward command post was located in the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you spoke about your military police battalion, and this is, for the record, in your testimony as of page 14878. Now, first of all, could you tell the Court how many military police battalions were there within the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade had two military police battalions called the 1st and the 2nd MP Battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Court, these two MP battalions, were they of equal size or did they differ in size?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: They were of different sizes. The 1st MP Battalion was larger, and its composition was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you describe the composition of your military police battalion, which was the 1st Military Police Battalion, on the same page in the Mrksic testimony. And you explain the various components besides the command, how you had various companies, communication section, crime section, et cetera. Could you give us a rough figure of the number of officers and soldiers in the 1st Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Roughly of the senior officers, that's to say, commissioned and non-commissioned officers, there were 120 of them, and around 800 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in relation to the 2nd Military Police Battalion, are you able to give us its strength?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: It had fewer men, and it only had three companies. So it had fewer men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. You don't have a rough figure in mind by any chance?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Approximately 500, and that's to say soldiers, commissioned and non-commissioned officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you explain in your Mrksic testimony - that's at page 14881 - how you were the deputy commander of the 1st Military Police Battalion but you replaced your commander when he became ill. Now, before assuming your role as acting commander of the 1st Military Police Battalion, how -- how familiar were you with the brigade commander, Mr. Mile Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I was quite familiar with him. I knew him, but I was not in daily contact with him. He contacted Major Kavalic. He was the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And as of the time when you become the acting deputy commander, how frequently were you in contact with the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: When I became the battalion commander, these contacts were daily. There was the daily briefing, and in the course of the day, we would be in contact, perhaps, twice or three times, or perhaps not once. But we had daily briefings at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: These daily briefings at 1800 hours, where did they take place?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: The briefings were held at Negoslavci, at the command post of the Guards Brigade or Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to take you now to the events of the 20th of November, 1991. You testified in the Mrksic case about the fact that sometime between 10.00 and 11.00 in the morning you received a call from Captain Predojevic, and you were told that there were problems about securing some buses with civilians at the barracks. For the record, this is at page 14889. Could you tell the Court how you were able to say that this took place somewhere between 10.00 and 11.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I'm able to say that because, based on my daily duties, and also when I was preparing for my first testimony, from conversations with all my various senior officers, I came to conclude that that was the time. I can't tell you exactly the -- the time in that time interval, but the interval is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And now, you -- you testify that you -- at that time you went to the site where the buses were and that you saw four or five buses surrounded by about 50 civilians and armed men. And these armed men you thought belonged to the Territorial Defence. For the record, this is at page 14890. Could you tell the Court where these TO members were from?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: These Territorial Defence members were from Vukovar. They were locals, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How were you able to come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I came to conclude that because they knew some of the people on the buses. They were talking about how some of these people had killed some of their own, torched their homes, chased their own people out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat the last sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, it appears that the interpreters weren't able to catch the last part of your answer. Could you repeat the last part of your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness come closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you're also asked to please come a little bit closer to the microphone so that they can hear you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: They knew some of them by name, and they said that they had killed some of their own family, set their houses on fire, or destroyed their houses, and persecuted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you testified that once you had observed the scene for about ten minutes, you returned to your building and you called your brigade commander. Now, where was your brigade commander located when you called him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: The brigade commander was at the command post at Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I would ask you to take a look at a footage we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P117.111. It's at tab 9 of our list. And I believe we have a very short translation for the interpreters. Okay. Are we ready to play?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let's play the clip please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "He stopped in Negoslavci for a short visit where he spoke to the commander of the operations group, Colonel Mile Mrksic and members of his staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise here the man at -- at the right-hand side at 18 minutes and 45 seconds of this clip?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I do, I recognise him. That's Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we rewind just a few seconds, please. Once more. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise the -- the building in the background?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: That building is the headquarters of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this is in which -- in which village or which town?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: It's the village of Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we keep playing, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, we see to the left side of the screen a number of soldiers here. Can you tell us who they are or what -- what unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: They are military police soldiers of the 1st Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: From this footage, are you able to tell us on -- on which occasion this -- this footage was recorded? Who is Mile Mrksic receiving?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I think that it was Cyrus Vance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And at the time while you were in Vukovar, were you familiar with the fact that Mr. Vance visited Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I was aware of that because the members of the 1st Battalion secured his visit from the moment he arrived, throughout his stay, and at his departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, earlier when I asked you if you recognised the building, you said that this is the headquarters of the Guards Brigade. So is this the building where Mr. Mrksic was located when you called him on the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we play the remainder of the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the premises that we're seeing on this footage at 18 minutes and 57 seconds?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: It's the operations room where we had our meetings at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is the village of Negoslavci, 3 kilometres south of Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we pause? Sorry. Can we just -- can you rewind a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- a bit more. Pause there. One more. Yeah, that's fine. Let's just leave it. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this international delegation, Mr. Susic, how were they able to enter the zone of -- of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Every visit was announced. Security would be readied so that during their stay in the area of the Guards Brigade they would be fully secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And who would need to announce themselves before entering your zone?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: All those who were not members of the Guards Brigade, including delegations, such as this one, visits by anyone from the state leadership, or anyone from other units; senior officers and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you testified in the Mrksic case that Mrksic ordered you to secure the buses - now we're back at the barracks on the 20th of November, 1991 - and he told you, and I quote from page 14891, that: "Now, the meeting of the government of Krajina is under way at which the question of where the buses will be transported is being resolved." Now, can you tell us if you're able to say what is meant here by "the Krajina government"?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he had in mind, but it referred to the government of that place, and that was Vukovar. So that would mean the civilian authorities of Vukovar, or the government of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how are you able to connect Vukovar to the term "Krajina government"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object because, as far as I understand, Mrksic mentioned the Krajina government, so I don't know why this question was put to the witness, how the witness connected Krajina government -- Vukovar with the term "Krajina government."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The question is about the witness's understanding. He was an interlocutor in the conversation and when the -- when his commander told him that there was a Krajina government meeting, it is relevant for him to tell us what he understood by that, and he already provided us half the answer by connecting it to the Vukovar government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, it is asked -- asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, let me ask my question again. Are you -- how are you able to connect Vukovar to the term "Krajina government"?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the civilian authorities. That's all. I didn't know what it was all about at the time, but I knew that they were referring to the civilian authority in that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, did Colonel Mrksic tell you where this meeting was taking place?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did you ever come to find out where this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, here in the transcript at page 14891, the word "government meeting" is -- is used, and I want to ask you if the term "meeting" is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I did not hear any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question. In the Mrksic case, the words "government meeting" is used, and I seek your clarification as to whether the term "meeting" is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, no, it was a government session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say "government session," are these your words, or are these the words of Mr. Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Those of Mr. Mrksic because he said that the government -- the session of the government of Krajina was in progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now at page 14893 of your Mrksic testimony, you testified that in order to take control of the situation at the barracks, you issued a verbal warning to the civilians and the TO members, and you increased the strength of the military police. By -- by how many military policemen did you increase the level of the troops?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: There were about 20 military police overall. And after a warning, they went away and did not return by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And I have one last topic for you, Mr. Susic. You spoke about Mr. Mrksic and -- being as -- commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade in OG South during the Vukovar operation. Can you tell the Court to whom was Mile Mrksic reporting during this time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: He was reporting to the command of the 1st Army because that's what they belonged to then, and to the General Staff, through the representative of the General Staff. That was Colonel Pavkovic. But I'm not familiar with any other details because I was not a member of the Guards Brigade Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And by "General Staff," what do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I mean the General Staff of the army, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And during normal circumstances, to whom did the Guards Motorised Brigade report to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances, it was directly subordinated to the General Staff. But at that moment when there were combat activities and there was the 1st Army, they were subordinated to the commander of the 1st Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Susic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Susic. My name is Zoran Zivanovic. I'm Goran Hadzic's Defence attorney in this trial. I'm going to ask you a few questions about the testimony you gave today and your testimony in the Mrksic case. You said today that Major Lukic became barracks commander in October 1991. Did he remain in that position until the Guards Brigade left on the 24th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain. You said what it meant for the barracks commander to be an also the commander of the 2nd Battalion or the 2nd Assault Detachment. Does that mean that he was present in the barracks, that he had his office there, that he stayed and slept there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. His command post was at the barracks, and as barracks commander, he was fully responsible for the entire security of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that he did not have offices at Negoslavci or that he didn't sleep there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: He did not sleep there. He slept at the barracks in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were deputy commander of the 1st Battalion of the military police until the 1st of November, 1991. And according to what I was able to read in your previous statement, it follows that that unit was a part of the 2nd Assault Detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No. The 1st Military Police Battalion secured the command post at Negoslavci, and one part secured the the rear command post at Berak. And one part was used to escort convoys from Negoslavci to Sid and back, or to Berak where the commander was. The 2nd Company of military police APCs from the 4th of October until the 24th of November was part of the 2nd Assault Battalion. And the anti-terrorist company from the 2nd to the 20th of October was part of the 2nd Assault Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You may know, but at any rate, we have information that the 2nd Military Police Battalion was not used in combat activities until the 1st of November; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: The anti-terrorist company was used from the 2nd until the 20th and then it was withdrawn to rest until the 1st, because, on the 1st, the anti-terrorist company and part of the military police company made up the 5th Assault Detachment, of which I was the commander, and it -- its place was between the 1st and the 2nd Assault Detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about the numerical strength of the 1st Battalion, you mentioned 120 officers and 8 00 soldiers. In the Mrksic case you said 900 soldiers but that difference doesn't matter so much now. Did you take into account that part of the 1st Battalion of military police that was part of the 2nd Assault Detachment, that is, the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was also a 2nd Military Police Battalion. Can you tell me who the commander was?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Major Radoje Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Today you spoke about the briefing at Negoslavci that you attended as of the 1st of November, 1991. Can you now tell us what was discussed at those briefings.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: At those briefings, the activities of that day were briefly analysed and tasks were assigned for the coming period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That briefing was attended by all battalion commanders from the 1st Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, all battalion commanders, members of the brigade command, and the brigade commander attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At those briefings, the subordinate officers, did they inform the brigade commander about what they did to carry out the orders on that -- the orders received on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is how it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And orders were also given for the coming day or days.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about Mladen Predojevic. What was his position in the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Mladen Predojevic was commander of the 2nd APC Company of the military police, and that company was attached to the 2nd Assault Battalion, and he secured the barracks with his men. I was with him from the 4th until the 1st, when I was appointed commander. And together with them, I defined the elements of barracks security; sentries, observation posts, gates, patrols, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The 2nd APC Company, the commander of which he was, was -- belonged to the 1st Battalion of military police.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. But then it became part of the 2nd Assault Battalion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the dates for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: The 2nd APC Company became part of the 2nd Assault Battalion on the 4th of November -- sorry, the 2nd -- the 4th of October until the 24th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During that time, it was subordinated to Major Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that Mladen Predojevic is no longer alive. Do you know when he died?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: He was killed in action in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In another trial, and here, too, you said that he contacted you on the 20th of November between 10 and 1100 hours. Can you please summarise that conversation for us.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Between 10 and 1100 hours, he called me to tell me that he was having problems because buses with some people had arrived, and the civilians had -- and civilians had gathered around them. And I was invited to go over there to see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I just wanted you to give us a short summary of the conversation. Later on, we'll move on to what happened later.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: He said that some buses with civilians had entered the barracks and that a group of people had gathered to protest and that something -- some unwanted events could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is all that he said to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask him why he was calling you at all?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask him why. Because he wouldn't have called me if he hadn't had a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can tell from that conversation, he didn't ask you to do anything.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, he did. He asked me to help him. That's what he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he state that explicitly or was that your conclusion from the conversation as you related it to us, that this must have been a request for help?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly how, but then I concluded that he needed help and that I had to go there to see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you went over to see what was happening. And can you tell us what you saw when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: When I arrived, I saw some four to five buses, one behind the other, and there were civilians on those buses. The drivers were in the driver's seats, and on the buses at the front and rear doors, there were police officers; one in the front, the other at the rear. Around them, there was a group of people, about 50, dressed in all sorts of ways, civilian clothes or civilian pants and uniform jackets and what have you. There was also a small number of them who were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said "civilians," were they men, women, children, elderly people?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: They were middle-aged. I didn't pay much attention, but I don't think I saw a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Children?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No children.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that you noticed police, did you mean military police?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, military police. But they weren't members of the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. But these were from the hospital, and the 2nd Battalion secured the hospital. They would probably have been soldiers of the 2nd Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that they were securing the hospital, how did you find out about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew that the 2nd Battalion was securing the hospital. It started on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you find out that the civilians were from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I asked the driver when I arrived, and the first one I met, I asked him, Where are you from? And he replied, These people are from the hospital. And that was confirmed also by Mladen Predojevic, and he said that he had learned that from the driver. And Major Vukasinovic had also been there, but I didn't meet him because we weren't there at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As you know that Paunovic was commander of the 2nd Military Police Battalion that was securing the hospital, why didn't you contact him to learn what all that was about and until what time he intended to send prisoners from the hospital to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I did not contact him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since all that was happening at the barracks, the commander of which was Major Lukic, can you tell me why you didn't contact him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I didn't contact him because this had to be taken care of immediately. I later saw Major Lukic. He -- later on, he was even -- there was even a Lieutenant-Colonel Panic at the barracks, the Chief of Staff. But after that, the situation was calm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you didn't contact him because you took immediate steps.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Correct. Since I was the one who set up security there, and since I was responsible, as of the 1st of November, together with Predojevic for the security of the barracks, I wanted to do that, rather than leave that to Predojevic. That's why I was looking to find a solution so that nothing untoward would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you set about doing it as soon as you arrived.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, as I got there, I went to have a look. I could have had the civilians removed at the time, but I didn't know what was going to happen to the buses. Were they going to stay there? Did we have any obligations towards these people, in terms of food, accommodation, and that was why I contacted the commander. I also wanted to know how long they would be staying there because, later on, we had to step up security and we didn't have enough men, so I wanted to know how many would have to be set aside for security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't discuss this with Predojevic, did you? I mean, where these buses were coming from, who sent them there, how long they would be staying there, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, Predojevic didn't know this. He didn't know this. He was told by the driver and, later on, by Major Vukasinovic that they had come from the hospital. And that much he knew. As I arrived, I asked the driver and then Predojevic confirmed that they had come, indeed, from the hospital, so I called the commander. I went back to the command post -- I mean, I went back to the command post, called the commander, and he told me specifically what the order was, and what I should be doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did Predojevic explain to you why didn't he inquire all of this himself? Why did he ask you to do so?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, he was unable to call the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And why?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, because he would be sidestepping his superior. He would have to have -- he would have to go through Major Lukic. And I don't know if he was there at the time or not. At any rate, he called me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't even try to get in touch with Lukic, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you have no explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No. Had Lukic been there, he would have sorted it out. Was he at the command post or somewhere else? I don't know. At any rate, I didn't ask about it, but Predojevic must have tried to call him, failed to get in touch with him, and then he contacted me, though I didn't ask him about all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how long was it after your conversation with Predojevic that you arrived at the place where the buses were?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, between my conversation with Predojevic and my arrival at the site, no more than five minutes passed. I was very close by, around 300 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And between your arrival there and your calling Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Some ten minutes. Well, I toured the buses there. I talked to the driver. I talked to Predojevic. I inspected the situation. So it could not have been longer than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how do you account for the fact that these 50 civilians and members of the TO ended up at the barracks? How were they able to gain access?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, there was the reception box, but they didn't go through the reception box. Rather, they went through the fence perimeter, which had been breached in many places by shells, et cetera. There were bits of it missing in places even, and so that's how they could gain access.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. So how did they get in?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, they went through the bits where the fence was missing and where there was no security. The perimeter around the barracks was quite large and you couldn't really deploy as many men as you would need to prevent people from entering.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And how were you able to know that they didn't go by the reception box?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I know simply by the fact that they would not have let them through, had they done this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know this for sure or do you assume this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I know this for sure because I deployed security, and they were tasked with not letting anyone through who had not previously been registered at the reception box.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me what the purpose of the reception box was to begin with, if anybody could gain access into the compound in the areas where the fencing was missing?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, everyone went through the reception box because that's where the road led. Those who wanted to gain access in a different way, they could have done so in the areas where -- not covered by security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, enemy units could have passed through there.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, they could not have. Because they would be acting differently. They would be acting from ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who would be acting differently?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, the security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that the security let them through?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, not really. But they could not physically prevent them from entering. They knew that they were not enemy soldiers. They knew that they were civilians, so I suppose they kind of thought this was going to be dealt with differently. They didn't use weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the 50 men, members of the Territorial Defence and civilians, gained access there because the security detail tolerated their entering the compound of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, they didn't tolerate it. They could not prevent them from entering. There were, let's say, two of them, and confronted with ten. And they didn't want to use weapons. They didn't want any killing there. They let them through, and then it was hoped that it would be resolved differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So that's what I'm saying: They actually let them through.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the time of your arrival at the place where the buses were and through to the departure of the buses, were you at the barracks all this time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No. As soon as we sorted it out and we did very soon with the orders and the warning, the mass of people left the barracks, and then when the buses left, I went back to my duties. There was a lot to do. I didn't have spare time to idle by the bus. But as I was moving in the compound, I saw Major Lukic and Lieutenant-Colonel Panic, Chief of Staff of the Guards Brigade there, and the situation was quite peaceful around the buses. No additional measures were required, save for the fact that the security around the barracks was stepped up to ensure that other people wouldn't gain access there again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long you stayed there, from the point you arrived? And I mean at the location where the buses were. How long did you stay there before leaving to attend to your other duties?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Between half an hour and 45 minutes. Because when I left the site, I didn't leave the barracks immediately. I was discussing how to set up the security detail with Predojevic. So, as I said, between 30 and 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go back to the place where the buses were later?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but I was passing by. Company commanders would be coming, groups of senior officers as well, and certain daily duties needed resolving. So I was around, and I was able to see the buses on a couple more occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say different senior officers were coming and you were dealing with various problems together with them. Were these problems related to the prisoners and these buses?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No. They were our daily duties. We were covering different locations, and we had to make our tasks very precise. At the same time, we were starting to prepare for our departure to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know up until when the buses stayed within the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, up until 1400 hours, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened then? Did you see the buses leave?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I saw the buses leave. They left. A colonel and a captain came with two all-terrain vehicles. They were received by Predojevic. Well, they went around the buses. They spoke to the drivers, and with one vehicle at the head of the column and the other at the rear, they set off for Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You witnessed this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, not really, but I was around. I was doing something else, and then, from a distance - perhaps 200 metres from the buses - I saw this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it because of the distance that you weren't able to hear what they were discussing?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't able to hear what they were saying. I didn't recognise the two. Had they come from the Guards Brigade, I would have recognised them. Obviously they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they come -- did they approach you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say you saw them from a distance of 200 metres from the buses. What I'd like to know is this: Predojevic, that colonel you mentioned, and the captain, were they by the buses?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were several buses. They passed by the buses, and then one of the vehicles was at the head, and then the other at the rear, and, in this way, they set off for Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you observe their entire conversation? I say "observe" because you weren't able to hear them. Did you observe them go around the buses? Did you observe the buses leave?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't looking at it all the time, but, yes, I would glance at them. And I was relieved to see the buses go because no more security would be required.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you observe any other senior officers from the Guards Brigade coming together with them, like Major Lukic or Panic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, not at the time, but in between they were. And then later on, they went to the command post at Lukic's. I don't know whether they were with Lukic or somewhere else, but they weren't there. Besides, I was dealing with my own duties, and this was something on the side, as it were, for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to describe for us the colonel that you saw that day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't know him. I only knew that he was active-duty colonel, because he had the rank of colonel. As for the captain, I concluded that he was TO because he had that SNB or olive-grey uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see whether the colonel was an elderly man or a young man?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, he was elderly, but I don't think I'd be able to recognise him if I saw him now. A colonel could not be younger than 40. If you call that old.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see if he was bald or if he had hair?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No. He had a cap on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have a moustache or something?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't able to observe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about his height? Was he as high -- as tall as Predojevic? Shorter?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you. I didn't pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they approach you at all? You say that you saw the buses. You saw them. This was at the distance of 200 metres. Did you come closer, or they?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No. I was busy doing something with senior officers. I wasn't at the command post itself. The command post was 300 metres away. But I was within the compound, talking to someone, one of the senior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that they didn't come closer at any point in order for you to get a better look?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how you were able to observe the rank of that person who was there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I was young, 34. I was able to see the rank from that distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that was how you were able to see the rank of captain as well.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Later Predojevic confirmed too. He said, The Colonel arrived or, A captain arrived, and so on. So he would have refreshed my memory, if I hadn't remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But, at any rate, you saw it with your own eyes.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that Predojevic later confirmed that, can you tell us what else you discussed with him when he told you that those people were a colonel and a captain? Did he tell you who they were or what -- what for and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew why they had come. And they left with the buses. The convoy moved on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that something is wrong with the transcript. No, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you knew why they had come. How come you knew? Who told you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: What do you mean who told me? I saw them leaving with the buses. So they came and continued with the convoy. That is, they attended that meeting and travelled on. The same buses, the same driver, the same security force. They continued moving fully secured so ... nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Predojevic tell you where they were going?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: He said towards Negoslavci, which I was able to see myself. It was the Negoslavci road that they took. Of course, they didn't tell him. Why would that colonel explain himself to a captain? We were a Guards Brigade. This captain received him. We visited the buses, and then they moved on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that Predojevic actually didn't know who that colonel was?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. He didn't know him. He wasn't a member of the Guards Brigade. He would know him otherwise. And we didn't have any colonels in that brigade, except for Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You know anybody in a colonel's uniform could have come and taken away whoever he wanted?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No way. Nobody else would have been able to come. Everything was known. You could tell that this was a JNA colonel and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that it was obvious. But you could tell from the uniform he was wearing and his rank insignia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. How could he have taken the whole security force and the buses? It would have been another thing if that man had come and put on some uniform, and those civilians had been taken from those buses to some other means of transportation. But given the fact that those were the very same buses with the very same drivers and the very same military police in military vehicles that were properly marked, an off-road vehicle at the head of the convoy and another at the tail-end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But why couldn't somebody else have the same kind of vehicle and attach plates to them, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Oh, well, come on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me: According to the rules that set out the -- that were in force for the work of the military police and the JNA, a military police unit is -- has a commander who is subordinated to the unit to which that military police unit belonged.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. The military police battalion was commanded by Major Kavalic. When he fell ill, I took over, and my superior was Commander Mrksic. And I was the superior of the company commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the rule-book --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I refer to P2761, paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This rule-book says, among other things, in paragraph 13 -- I mean, the rule-book of the military police. There are also provisions about the security organ also has the role of being in charge of the military police along professional lines. So what did that mean with regard to your military police battalion? I mean, the security organ.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, the key word here is "professional." So he makes proposals to the brigades commander and then the brigade commander decides. However, the security organ does not have the authority to issue orders. Only to propose things to the commander and then he -- he can issue orders. For example, to define some tasks, assign them to someone, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could the commander issue orders both personally and through the authorised security organ?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Only personally. He never did so through the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you, as military police battalion commander, were not in contact with the security organs?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I was. I always had contacts with them, but they could not issue me orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe those contacts with the security organs that you had? Or let us take the freshest event. The fall of Vukovar on the 18th of November, 1991. What kind of contacts with the security organs did you have then?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: We met at briefings and -- I don't know. If they came to inspect the unit, to see what the situation was like, and such occasions. But as for issuing orders, they couldn't do that. During the inspection, they could make some observations based on which they would make proposals to the commander, and the commander could then order some things to be rectified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was reading the rule-book we're discussing, and I noticed that one of the duties of the military police is escorting persons that -- deprived of liberty, among whom there are prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Correct. That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when did you that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: We did that on the 19th. For example, the battalion from Mitnica which surrendered on the 18th and it was disarmed and it was at Ovcara, and from Ovcara, we escorted them to Sremska Mitrovica on the 18th, and it was the 1st Military Police Company from the 1st Battalion who did that. And I prepared the people for that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "prepared," do you mean that you prepared the military police or the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I mean the unit. And a -- an officer is always given the task of preparing those to be transported. That is, making a list, and so on. The police gives -- provides security. There was a police officer at the front door, one at the rear door, and nobody was allowed to enter. And whoever was on the side couldn't possibly shoot or throw stones at the bus. But to prevent that, I called Colonel Mrksic to take steps to prevent that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that those prisoners from Mitnica were registered?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were all registered. A list was made, and with that list, they were handed over at Sremska Mitrovica. It was on the 19th of November. Because they surrendered on the 18th, they spent the night at Ovcara. In the evening of the 18th, I was given the task to prepare a unit to provide security. There were APCs and so on. In a word, they went to Sremska Mitrovica under full security and were handed over there. And we also escorted a convoy from Velepromet. They were escorted to the border but they wouldn't accept them. And then we had to go to Sid. And so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you personally didn't escort that convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No. But I gave orders, and they had to report to me later how everything had gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know about those people who were brought to the barracks on the 20th of November, if they had been registered?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know. But I'm sure that they were. Because whoever put them on the buses was duty-bound to make a list of them. Now who that was, I don't know, but it must have been that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have information that during -- or that while those buses were at the barracks, the prisoners were physically maltreated, were taken out of the buses, and that some of them were returned on some other bus. Have you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. And Captain Predojevic confirmed that Major Vukasinovic from the brigade command, who was the security organ, had come on a bus and taken some 20 people from the other buses, to return them. Major Vukasinovic did that. Now whether there were some physical contacts or not, I don't know because I wasn't there. After that, Predojevic called me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you don't know anything about the mistreatment of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I wasn't there, nor was I told that there was anything of the kind. But I was told that Major Vukasinovic had been there, and that he had taken away some 20 people. Whether anything happened while they were leaving isn't anything I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: About that convoy that the military police escorted to Sremska Mitrovica, can you tell me who issued that order?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Mrksic did. These are the briefings we were talking about. On the 18th, he ordered me to make preparations for the escort of a convoy of prisoners to Sremska Mitrovica, but to who he assigned the task to register them, to make a list, I don't know. Whether it was someone from the brigade command or not, but certainly someone would have had -- had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in the framework of OG South there was the 80th Motorised Brigade from Kragujevac?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I had no contacts with them. They were also at Ovcara to provide security. That was their zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that, given the fact that you attended all those briefings, town commanders were appointed, starting from Vukovar to other places, villages?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. The town commander at Negoslavci was Major Vukasinovic. Yes. But physical security was provided by the 1st Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what those town commanders were actually supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commanders were responsible for the overall security and safety and the activities at that place that was being secured. Who was coming, who was going, where the security was placed, and so on. I wasn't in that role, so I couldn't give you the details. But he cannot issue orders to the security but orders me -- or, rather, not me, but asks Mrksic for a reception box to be placed somewhere, or whatever, and then I make a decision based on a professional considerations where to place these.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When we say "town commander," I mean a village or a neighbourhood of a town or something?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, he was commander of Negoslavci, Major Vukasinovic. Major Lukic was a barracks commander. Whether there was some commander at Berak, for example, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Susic, this is the time for our first break. We'll take 30 minutes. We'll come back at 11.00. The court usher will show you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Susic, Colonel Mrksic was the commander of the Guards Brigade at the time of your arrival in Vukovar, which was the 30th of September, 1991, I believe; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, Operations Group South was set up, and he became its commander.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when he became the commander of the Operations Group South who became commander of the 1st Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: That was one and the same. It's just that that was -- that the name Operations Group South was used in combat. Other than that, he was the commander of both. That's why we sometimes mix up the two, the commander of the Guards Brigade and operations group, because it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Guards Brigade was declared to be Operations Group South or did it mean something else?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, you're right. The Guards Brigade was called Operations Group South. That was the task that it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In my understanding, the Operations Group South consisted of some other units in addition to the Guards Brigade. Does this mean that these other units were under the 1st Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Or under the operations group. Again, it's the same. The commander was Mrksic. There can be a difference, though. But these units joined the Operations Group South and were under the command of Mrksic. Later on, when the operations ended, they left that contingent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information I have, following Mrksic's appointment as commander Operations Group South, the commander of the 1st Guards Brigade was Miodrag Panic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No. Miodrag Panic was Chief of Staff of both the Guards Brigade and the operations group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of your arrival in the area of Vukovar, you were captain first class by rank; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when were you promoted to the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: That was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And to the rank of lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: That was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And, finally, to the rank of colonel?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when was the first time you heard - if at all - that a number of people were summarily shot at Ovcara? The people from hospital, and roughly 200 of them.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I learnt it from newspapers, and it was only two or three years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that after the return of the Guards Brigade on the 24th of November, you were still in touch with the people in the brigade. So you didn't hear from them of anything like that happening until 1996 or later?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, no. And I was part of the Guards Brigade within the battalion, up until 1994, when I went to attend schooling at the Staff Command, at the Command Staff Academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this Command Staff Academy is, so that the Trial Chamber may understand what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: The Command Staff Academy is a higher schooling institution which gives training to people up to the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you called by the organs of the then-JNA, and later by the Army of Yugoslavia, to give any statements relative to your participation in the events in Vukovar and about the events in Vukovar in general?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: It was either in 2000 or 2001 that the security organs called me, and I gave a statement similar to the one that I am giving now, about my work and such-like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D1098.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you can see that statement now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that's my signature at the bottom. It's my statement. It's not a very clear copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll enlarge it for you now and then we'll have a look at it in some detail. Tell me first: Is this the only statement you gave to the military security structure?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall who you talked to at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: The security organ, Petar Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was the security organ of the Guards Brigade at the time or some other unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he the chief of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was at the time of your discussion with him that this statement was made.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at paragraph 3 of your statement. And this is how it reads: "I declare under full responsibility that not a single member of the company under the command of late Captain Mladen Predojevic was involved in escorting the convoy outside the barracks, and that Captain Mladen Predojevic and his unit fully secured the buses carrying men while they were at the Vukovar barracks. Furthermore, officers and soldiers of his unit did not board the buses or in any way mistreat the civilians aboard these buses." You were able to follow?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, on reading this passage, one gains the impression that you were there at all times and, therefore, on the basis of your first-hand observations, you said that during their stay at the barracks, they were secured by men and that neither officers nor soldiers of his units boarded the buses or mistreated the civilians. You told us today that you you spent roughly 45 minutes there, at which point you left. What I'd like to know is this: On the basis of what did you tell the security organ that, at all times, while present at the barracks, members of Predojevic's unit, including himself, never boarded the buses or mistreated civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: During these 45 minutes I was there, after we had removed that group of civilians surrounding the buses, the situation was quite calm. Besides, both at the front and rear doors, there were military policemen based who did not leave that position. I was working within the compound. I wasn't there at all times, but I did observe occasionally that they did not approach the buses anymore. The buses were secured, and there was no way one could come close to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could anyone else mistreat them?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No, not during this time. It was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "not during this time," do you mean the 45 minutes or throughout their stay there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, for these 45 minutes after the arrival of that group of people, up until their departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, we have information to the effect that some of the civilians were mistreated, taken off the buses, that various people were involved in this, both uniformed and in civilian clothes, and it doesn't tally with what you're telling us. Did you hear of what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, when Vukasinovic -- and this was before this particular event, at the time when that group of people were still there. So when -- when he was still trying to turn people back from the bus, at that point in time, this could have happened. But later on, there was nobody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we have a look at paragraph 2 of your statement, line 2, where you say: I declare under full responsibility that the men did not leave the buses but were waiting for other buses ... to gather (about five to six buses). Next a convoy was formed out of these buses and under the command of two individuals, one of whom a colonel (unknown to me) and a member of the Vukovar TO, the column was taken charge of and under escort by the military police, taken somewhere, I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they took the road to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm also interested in another thing you said. The individuals on the buses were waiting for other buses to gather, some five to six. It is not quite consistent with what you are saying here. You said that the buses were already there.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you see, they were expecting some other buses to arrive, and that's why they were waiting there. However, no more buses came.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And who was it who was expecting other buses to come?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: They came there in order for a complete convoy to be made. That's why they stopped there. I don't know what other expectations they had, but they were there until roughly 2.00 p.m. And then that same column of vehicles left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did somebody tell you that they were waiting for extra buses?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I spoke to the driver and was told that they were assembling there and that they would then continue their journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's another thing that strikes me when reading this statement of yours. You're not mentioning any sort of conversation with Mrksic here, or any part of your communication with him or what he told you.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, this was certainly the case because I was not put such a question. I was answering the questions that he put to me, and if he had asked me that, I would certainly have told him that I had a discussion with the commander where -- and what we talked about and at what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you were merely answering the questions put to you by Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: That's correct. He put questions to me, and I answered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, didn't he know that Predojevic was commander of the 2nd Company of the military police? Did he ask you about it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the way he formed his question. He must have known. He was at the Guards Brigade at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about the first paragraph of your statement. Did he ask you who Predojevic was subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because Kovacevic did not go to Vukovar. He was at the barracks in Dedinje at the time these combat operations were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he ask you about the civilians being brought over from the hospital in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the statement is based on him putting questions to me and me giving the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, he did ask you about the civilians being brought over from the hospital in Vukovar or not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I know that when he put a question to me, I answered it and the answer was recorded here. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So did he ask you where these civilians had come from and why they were brought over? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You do recall your testimony in the Mrksic case?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You remember that Mrksic's Defence challenged the very fact that you talked to Mrksic on that day and at that time and about that subject.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I share their view and believe that this conversation did not take place the way you say it did, do you know that at the time you say you spoke to Mr. Mrksic, no government meeting was taking place?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know if there was a meeting or not, nor who chaired it, or where it was held. What I know for a fact is that this is what the commander, Colonel Mrksic, told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that's what he told you then, between 10 and 1100 hours?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Prosecutor back then, in that trial, asked you who had taken those people from the barracks, and you replied that you didn't know. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I did not say that I didn't know who, but, rather, that I didn't know that colonel or that captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I refer to P3026, page 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, while this document is coming up, I'm looking at your guide-lines here, and I understand -- I don't want to get too technical, but I understand that for cross-examination of a 92 ter witness, the opposing party usually has double, 200 per cent. I think we're way over that time. So can we seek some clarification as to where the Defence is heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I have just few minutes to finish my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And do you remember that the Prosecutor claimed then that both you and many others knew who had taken the prisoners to Ovcara but that you were concealing that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he was saying. But I said then, and I am saying now, that I don't know and that I'm not concealing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you haven't found out to this day.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Susic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
